headline: Trump's chief of staff says she is cancer-free
summary: White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles said Wednesday she is free of cancer, six months to the day after announcing her diagnosis. She wrote on X that her pathology tests "came back clear" after a visit to the Mayo Clinic this week. Wiles, 69, kept working from home through six months of treatment. She is the first woman to hold the job.

cover_question.q: How do they know the cancer is gone?

cover_answer: Tests. Her pathology results came back clear.
table_question: When you get good news, who do you tell first?

5-7.script: A woman who helps run the White House was sick with cancer for six months. Today she said her tests came back clear, which means the doctors can't find any cancer now. She kept doing her job from home the whole time, like doing schoolwork on a sick day. The grown-ups took good care of her.
5-7.why: Sick, then better, is a story a six-year-old already knows. The sick day keeps it small.

8-12.script: In March, Susie Wiles, the president's chief of staff, said she had breast cancer. She had six months of treatment and worked from home. This week her tests came back clear. A test like that is a report card: it shows what doctors can find right now.
8-12.why: Diagnosis, treatment, test, result. A chain they can follow.

13-17.script: Would you keep working through cancer treatment? Susie Wiles, Trump's chief of staff, did, from home, for six months, and posted the all-clear on X Wednesday. In March she said one in eight women are diagnosed with breast cancer. Why say that out loud?
13-17.why: Teens know someone who has had cancer. Let them name that person first.

5-7.a: Her tests came back clear, so the doctors found no cancer. She kept working the whole time and says she will keep going.

8-12.q: How do they know the cancer is gone?
8-12.a: Tests at the Mayo Clinic this week. Her pathology results came back clear.

8-12.q: What is a chief of staff?
8-12.a: The president's gatekeeper and planner. Wiles is the first woman in the job.

13-17.q: Would you keep working through cancer treatment?
13-17.a: She did, from home, for six months. Her post gave no treatment details.

13-17.q: Why do you think she said that out loud?
13-17.a: In March she said one in eight women are diagnosed, and now she joins their ranks.
